To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the smartphone provider can provide a solution that will not only satisfy the security agencies but also the independent users who are concerned about the privacy of their data, (ii) the solution is not very difficult to implement and can be implemented in a way that it does not affect the performance of the system, and (iii) the solution does not violate the security of the system.

(i) there is a way to intercept and analyze data leaving the enterprise servers without breaking the end-to-end encryption and without any involvement of the smartphone provider, and (ii) this can be done by using the existing infrastructure of the enterprise servers.

(a) the smartphone provider can provide the security agencies with an option to intercept the data leaving their jurisdiction, (b) such interception can be done without compromising the privacy of the users, and (c) such interception can take place only when the data is in transit and not when it is in rest.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following issues: (1) the feasibility of a solution that will allow a sovereignty to intercept encrypted email messages of its citizens and (2) the impact of the solution on the privacy of its citizens.

the following: (a) analyzing the data flow between the smartphone and the enterprise server, and (b) proposing a solution that can be acceptable to both the parties, the smartphone provider and the enterprise, and at the same time can address the concerns of the sovereignty.
the following issues: (i) the security issues of smartphone data flows and (ii) the possible solutions to these issues, which are acceptable to both parties.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, if the sovereignty concerned is willing to provide the smartphone provider a lawful access to its encrypted data, then it should be able to provide a solution that is technically feasible, legally sound and acceptable to both the parties concerned.

the security agencies should not be concerned about encrypted data leaving their jurisdictions as the data is not encrypted at the source and is encrypted only after it leaves the jurisdiction and is on its way to global smartphone routers.

, the smartphone provider can provide the security agencies of the concerned sovereignties with a solution, which would allow them to intercept the data flow in an unencrypted form while the users would still remain unaware of this fact.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have identified the threat and proposed solutions that are acceptable to all parties concerned, viz., the user, the corporate, and the security agencies.

we propose a mechanism that allows the sovereignty’s security agencies to have a lawful intercept on the encrypted data that is leaving the country, while ensuring that the smartphone provider’s customers do not lose their privacy.

the proposed solutions would allow the security agencies of these sovereignty nations to intercept encrypted data, while the smartphones continue to be secure and provide privacy to their independent customers.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in the current state, the smartphone data is encrypted in transit, but not at rest.
the proposed solutions are simple to implement and do not involve any significant change to the existing smartphone data transfer protocols.
it provides an insight to the smartphone industry and the security agencies about the possible ways to address the issues raised by the latter.
